textbookSource.author: Hal Blumenfeld
textbookSource.title: Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases

textbookSource.pageMapping: Printed body page N = physical N+26; labels checked in extracted headers and original rendered pages.

method.application: Every132 assigned structure records and26 syndrome cards reread in full. Exact originals pinned to baseline git blobs to avoid root-edit drift. Names/synonyms, functions, clinical claims/laterality, connections, supply, relative location covered.
method.textbook: Complete relevant extracted text read. Original figures inspected privately with pypdfium2. Family page anchors identify coverage, not precision support for every detailed claim.
method.public: Each proposed correction has public cross-validation. Human/animal evidence distinguished. Some NCBI opens faced challenge screens; precise indexed abstracts supplied corroboration where full open unavailable.

findings.originalValue: Ia muscle-spindle and periodontal afferents of CN V that bypass the trigeminal ganglion and descend via the mesencephalic tract
findings.proposedReplacement: Peripheral processes of mesencephalic trigeminal primary sensory neurons carry jaw-muscle-spindle and periodontal input through CN V; their cell bodies lie in the CNS rather than the trigeminal ganglion.
findings.explanation: Incoming peripheral proprioceptive processes are confused with descending central reflex processes. The book separates peripheral input from processes descending to motor V; periodontal afferents are not all Ia muscle-spindle fibers.

textbookEvidence.supportSummary: Incoming peripheral proprioceptive processes are confused with descending central reflex processes. The book separates peripheral input from processes descending to motor V; periodontal afferents are not all Ia muscle-spindle fibers.

publicEvidence.title: Wang and May 2008, MesV peripheral targets and central projections
publicEvidence.supportSummary: CNS primary sensory somata; peripheral processes exit through the trigeminal motor root, while central processes descend and give motor-system collaterals.
publicEvidence.limitations: Detailed tracing is macaque evidence, not established human synaptic mapping.

publicEvidence.title: Clinical Methods, Cranial Nerve V
publicEvidence.supportSummary: Separates primary afferent peripheral processes from central MesV processes descending to motor V.

findings.originalValue: Relay of the lateral (cerebellar) motor system in the rostral midbrain tegmentum. The caudal magnocellular part is the origin of the rubrospinal tract, which crosses immediately in the ventral tegmentum and facilitates flexor tone of the contralateral limbs; the rostral parvocellular part links the cerebellum with the inferior olive through the central tegmental tract (rubro-olivary, Guillain-Mollaret loop) and subserves motor learning. In humans the rubrospinal system is vestigial relative to the corticospinal tract, but the nucleus remains a major dentatorubrothalamic relay.
findings.proposedReplacement: Motor-related nucleus of the rostral midbrain tegmentum. Its caudal magnocellular division gives rise to the crossed rubrospinal pathway, much less developed in humans than in many other mammals. Its rostral parvocellular division receives cerebellar and cortical inputs and projects to the ipsilateral inferior olive through the central tegmental tract. Cerebellothalamic fibers also pass through or around the red-nucleus region en route to the thalamus; these differ from fibers terminating in the red nucleus.
findings.explanation: The original final sentence implies a major required dentatorubrothalamic nuclear relay, contradicting the corrected connections. Fig15.9 separates direct cerebellothalamic fibers continuing to VL from RN termination and the rubro-olivary limb.

textbookEvidence.supportSummary: The original final sentence implies a major required dentatorubrothalamic nuclear relay, contradicting the corrected connections. Fig15.9 separates direct cerebellothalamic fibers continuing to VL from RN termination and the rubro-olivary limb.

publicEvidence.title: Gallay et al. 2008, Human cerebellothalamic and pallidothalamic tracts
publicEvidence.supportSummary: Cerebellothalamic fibers connect deep cerebellar nuclei with thalamus, crossing in the SCP and passing through/anterior to the red nucleus before thalamic entrance.
publicEvidence.limitations: Histology maps tract course. Detailed target circuitry also draws on monkey tracing; the correction does not deny all possible rubrothalamic projections.

findings.originalValue: Composite fiber systems of the basis pontis: the longitudinal fasciculi carry corticospinal, corticobulbar and corticopontine axons from the crus cerebri down to the medulla, while the transverse fibers arise from the pontine nuclei, decussate, and collect laterally as the middle cerebellar peduncle.
findings.proposedReplacement: Composite fiber systems of the basis pontis: longitudinal fasciculi contain corticospinal axons continuing toward the medulla, corticobulbar axons reaching their brainstem targets, and corticopontine axons terminating in the pontine nuclei. Transverse pontocerebellar fibers arise from pontine neurons, cross the midline, and collect laterally as the middle cerebellar peduncle.
findings.explanation: Corticopontine fibers synapse in pons; corticobulbar axons reach respective brainstem targets. Only corticospinal fibers in this list continue as a common system to medulla.

textbookEvidence.supportSummary: Corticopontine fibers synapse in pons; corticobulbar axons reach respective brainstem targets. Only corticospinal fibers in this list continue as a common system to medulla.

publicEvidence.title: Tredici et al. 1990, Organization of corticopontine fibres in man
publicEvidence.supportSummary: Discusses cortical projections to pontine nuclei and their internal-capsular route. Supports pontine termination, rather than obligatory continuation to medulla.
publicEvidence.limitations: Does not precisely validate all traditional peduncular fiber partitions.

findings.originalValue: Medial crus infarction with CN III fascicles: ipsilateral pupil-involving CN III palsy plus contralateral face-arm-leg hemiplegia.
findings.proposedReplacement: A medial cerebral-peduncle lesion involving CN III fascicles can cause ipsilateral third-nerve palsy with contralateral motor weakness (Weber pattern); completeness, pupil involvement, and weakness distribution or severity depend on lesion extent.
findings.explanation: The book table gives weakness plus third palsy; fascicular discussion allows partial deficits. Pupil involvement and complete face-arm-leg hemiplegia are not obligatory.

textbookEvidence.supportSummary: The book table gives weakness plus third palsy; fascicular discussion allows partial deficits. Pupil involvement and complete face-arm-leg hemiplegia are not obligatory.

publicEvidence.title: Clinical Methods, Cranial Nerves III, IV, VI
publicEvidence.supportSummary: Separate midbrain fascicles often cause partial III dysfunction; ventral corticospinal involvement causes crossed hemiparesis (Weber pattern).

findings.originalValue: A lesion at the facial colliculus damages the abducens nucleus and the looping facial fibers together — ipsilateral conjugate gaze palsy plus complete LMN facial paralysis (Foville syndrome), with loss of the ipsilateral blink.
findings.proposedReplacement: A focal lesion involving the abducens nucleus and looping facial fibers can cause ipsilateral horizontal conjugate gaze palsy and lower motor neuron facial weakness, including impaired eyelid closure. The full classic Foville pattern adds contralateral body weakness when descending motor pathways are also involved; focal dorsal lesions need not include that component.
findings.explanation: The dorsal VI-nucleus/VII-genu landmark does not automatically define the full basis-and-tegmentum Foville syndrome; completeness depends on extent.

textbookEvidence.supportSummary: The dorsal VI-nucleus/VII-genu landmark does not automatically define the full basis-and-tegmentum Foville syndrome; completeness depends on extent.

publicEvidence.title: Zhuang et al. 2021, Bilateral facial colliculus syndrome
publicEvidence.supportSummary: Dorsal pontine colliculus infarcts produced facial paralysis and horizontal gaze palsy with limb strength5/5. Shows focal dorsal VI-VII dysfunction need not include crossed body weakness.
publicEvidence.limitations: One case establishes a possibility, not frequency.

publicEvidence.title: Foville Syndrome, NCBI Bookshelf
publicEvidence.supportSummary: Classic inferior medial pontine syndrome combines ipsilateral gaze/VI and facial dysfunction with contralateral hemiparesis; variants exist.

findings.originalValue: AICA (caudal) and SCA (rostral) short circumferential branches of the basilar artery
findings.proposedReplacement: Predominantly AICA branches, with SCA contributions and variable territorial overlap or anastomoses.
findings.explanation: AICA/SCA are long circumferential cerebellar systems, not the short circumferential branches stated in the original. Territorial division varies.

textbookEvidence.supportSummary: AICA/SCA are long circumferential cerebellar systems, not the short circumferential branches stated in the original. Territorial division varies.

publicEvidence.evidenceType: Primary human four-case series with anatomy discussion
publicEvidence.supportSummary: Describes predominant AICA supply and SCA contributions/anastomotic overlap; does not support rigid universal territory boundaries.
publicEvidence.limitations: Selected clinical cases are not a population vascular map.

findings.originalValue: Transsynaptic degeneration of the olive after a lesion of the Guillain-Mollaret triangle (dentate nucleus, superior cerebellar peduncle, or central tegmental tract), producing palatal (palatopharyngeal) myoclonus/tremor months after the index lesion.
findings.proposedReplacement: Disruption of afferent dentato-olivary pathways, such as dentate/superior cerebellar peduncle or central tegmental tract injury, can cause transsynaptic olivary degeneration. Delayed palatal or oculopalatal tremor may develop, but is not present in every case.
findings.explanation: Book associates the loop with palatal tremor; human pathology shows it is not an inevitable consequence of pathway injury.

textbookEvidence.supportSummary: Book associates the loop with palatal tremor; human pathology shows it is not an inevitable consequence of pathway injury.

publicEvidence.title: Nishie et al. 2002, Palatal tremor and olivary hypertrophy
publicEvidence.supportSummary: Only8 of16 subjects with dentate-olivary cerebrovascular pathway lesions had symptomatic palatal tremor. Pathological change evolved and later olivary neuronal loss was extensive.

findings.originalValue: MRI shows T2 hyperintensity with enlargement of the olive (hypertrophic degeneration, not atrophy).
findings.proposedReplacement: MRI findings evolve with time: T2 hyperintensity may precede visible olivary enlargement, enlargement may develop later and then resolve, and signal abnormality may persist. Olivary size is not enlarged at every stage.

textbookEvidence.supportSummary: Original makes T2 hyperintensity plus enlargement obligatory and excludes atrophy. Human MRI/pathology show stage-dependent enlargement, resolution, and later neuronal loss.

publicEvidence.supportSummary: T2 signal preceded enlargement; enlargement developed later and resolved over several years while signal could persist. Enlargement is not obligatory at every stage.
publicEvidence.limitations: Pooled selected cases do not impose an exact individual timeline.

publicEvidence.supportSummary: Only8 of16 subjects with dentate-olivary cerebrovascular pathway lesions had symptomatic palatal tremor. Pathological change evolved and later olivary neuronal loss was extensive.
publicEvidence.limitations: Selected autopsy cohort; not a prevalence estimate.

findings.proposedReplacement: Tuberothalamic (polar) artery, usually from the posterior communicating artery; paramedian PCA supply may substitute when the polar artery is absent.
findings.explanation: The clinical label incorrectly assigns named tuberothalamic artery to PCA while bloodSupply correctly says PCoA. Book supplies broad deep-vessel context; human anatomy resolves the named origin.

textbookEvidence.supportSummary: The clinical label incorrectly assigns named tuberothalamic artery to PCA while bloodSupply correctly says PCoA. Book supplies broad deep-vessel context; human anatomy resolves the named origin.

publicEvidence.title: Percheron1976, Human polar thalamic artery
publicEvidence.supportSummary: The polar/tuberothalamic artery arises from PCoA, is present variably, and supplies rostral thalamic territory toward the mammillothalamic tract.

findings.originalValue: Acute anterograde amnesia, apathy, abulia and executive dysfunction; left-sided lesions add an 'aphasia-plus' state and right-sided lesions neglect, because the Papez circuit is interrupted at the anterior nucleus.
findings.proposedReplacement: Anterior/tuberothalamic territory infarction can cause impaired new learning, apathy or abulia, and executive or orientation difficulties. Dominant-side lesions may affect language and nondominant-side lesions visuospatial attention; these depend on the nuclei and pathways involved and are not attributable to the anterior nucleus alone.
findings.explanation: Variable language/neglect territory effects are incorrectly attributed entirely to Papez interruption at one anterior nucleus. Territory includes other thalamic structures and disconnections.

textbookEvidence.supportSummary: Variable language/neglect territory effects are incorrectly attributed entirely to Papez interruption at one anterior nucleus. Territory includes other thalamic structures and disconnections.

publicEvidence.title: Schmahmann2003, Vascular syndromes of thalamus
publicEvidence.supportSummary: Tuberothalamic injury affects memory, executive/personality/arousal functions; dominant language effects depend partly on VL involvement and nondominant effects include visuospatial deficits.
publicEvidence.limitations: Territory effects are not attributable to the anterior nucleus alone.

findings.originalValue: Thiamine deficiency damages the anterior thalamic nuclei together with the mammillary bodies, producing dense anterograde amnesia with confabulation.
findings.proposedReplacement: Thiamine-deficiency injury can involve mammillary bodies and thalamic/periventricular memory networks, including anterior and medial thalamus. Persistent Korsakoff amnesia may severely impair new learning; confabulation can occur and is variable.
findings.explanation: Original compresses distributed variable injury into mandatory two-node damage and confabulation. Book discusses medial diencephalic/periventricular injury and says patients often confabulate.

textbookEvidence.supportSummary: Original compresses distributed variable injury into mandatory two-node damage and confabulation. Book discusses medial diencephalic/periventricular injury and says patients often confabulate.

publicEvidence.title: Harding et al.2000, Anterior thalamic degeneration and alcoholic amnesia
publicEvidence.evidenceType: Primary human postmortem stereology; university abstract
publicEvidence.supportSummary: Mammillary/MD loss occurred in amnesic and non-amnesic Wernicke cases; anterior thalamic loss differentiated alcoholic Korsakoff amnesia. Supports distributed circuitry.
publicEvidence.limitations: Alcohol-associated cohort; not all causes of thiamine deficiency.

publicEvidence.title: Kessels et al.2008, Confabulation in Korsakoff syndrome
publicEvidence.supportSummary: Measured variable spontaneous/provoked confabulation, source memory, executive function. Confabulation is not interchangeable with amnesia.

findings.originalValue: Obligatory relay of retinal vision to cortex: six layers receive a strictly retinotopic, eye-segregated map (ipsilateral eye 2/3/5, contralateral 1/4/6), with magnocellular layers serving motion and parvocellular layers form and color, forwarded to V1 via the retrolenticular internal capsule. Pupil-light-reflex fibers leave the optic tract before the LGN, so LGN lesions spare the light reflex.
findings.proposedReplacement: Principal relay of the geniculostriate visual pathway to primary visual cortex: six layers receive a strictly retinotopic, eye-segregated map (ipsilateral eye 2/3/5, contralateral 1/4/6), with magnocellular layers serving motion and parvocellular layers form and color, forwarded to V1 via the retrolenticular internal capsule. Pupil-light-reflex fibers leave the optic tract before the LGN, so an isolated LGN lesion can spare the light reflex. Other retinal projections, including superior-collicular/pulvinar pathways, do not require the LGN as their relay.
findings.explanation: LGN is the principal geniculostriate relay, not obligatory for all retinal signals reaching all cortex. Book describes retinal-SC-pulvinar-extrastriate route; macaque experiment corroborates it without presuming detailed human function.

textbookEvidence.supportSummary: LGN is the principal geniculostriate relay, not obligatory for all retinal signals reaching all cortex. Book describes retinal-SC-pulvinar-extrastriate route; macaque experiment corroborates it without presuming detailed human function.

publicEvidence.title: Berman and Wurtz2010, SC-pulvinar-MT pathway
publicEvidence.supportSummary: Pulvinar relay neurons received SC input and projected to MT, establishing a continuous extrastriate pathway outside the geniculostriate relay.
publicEvidence.limitations: Macaque findings; detailed role in individual human vision not presumed.

findings.originalValue: Rhythm and stress-coordination nucleus linking the suprachiasmatic clock to feeding and sleep-wake cycles: DMH neurons generate anticipatory locomotor and feeding rhythms and recruit endocrine (paraventricular) and autonomic outputs during stress.
findings.proposedReplacement: Hypothalamic nucleus participating in circadian, feeding, stress, endocrine, and autonomic networks. Animal studies implicate DMH circuits in coordinating sleep-wake/physiological outputs and modulating meal anticipation; they do not establish a necessary food-anticipatory rhythm generator in humans.
findings.explanation: Unqualified generation claim upgrades disputed rodent models into settled human function. Book gives network context; rat lesion studies show retained anticipation without DMH.

textbookEvidence.supportSummary: Unqualified generation claim upgrades disputed rodent models into settled human function. Book gives network context; rat lesion studies show retained anticipation without DMH.

publicEvidence.title: Landry et al.2011, DMH lesions and food anticipation
publicEvidence.supportSummary: Rats with partial/complete DMH ablation retained meal anticipation; effects depended on time of day, supporting modulation rather than a necessary generator.
publicEvidence.limitations: Rodent evidence; human food-anticipation generator unestablished.

findings.originalValue: Myelinated limbic afferent bundle sweeping along the dorsomedial border of the thalamus from the septal/preoptic region to the habenular nuclei — the principal input limb of the epithalamic circuit feeding the anti-reward system.
findings.proposedReplacement: Limbic afferent bundle running along the dorsomedial thalamic border from septal, preoptic, basal-forebrain, and hypothalamic regions to the habenular complex. Medial and lateral habenular circuits have distinct inputs and outputs; the entire bundle is not a single anti-reward pathway.
findings.explanation: Anatomical pathway is sound but anti-reward label conflates medial/lateral circuits and contradicts revised adjacent habenula record.

textbookEvidence.supportSummary: Anatomical pathway is sound but anti-reward label conflates medial/lateral circuits and contradicts revised adjacent habenula record.

publicEvidence.title: Parent et al.1981, Forebrain afferents to habenula
publicEvidence.supportSummary: Shows distributed hypothalamic/preoptic/septal/basal-forebrain afferents and species differences. Anatomical input is broader than one anti-reward system.
publicEvidence.limitations: Tracing does not establish each pathway psychological role in humans.

publicEvidence.title: Hikosaka et al.2008, Habenula basal-ganglia/limbic crossroads
publicEvidence.supportSummary: Separates medial septal/interpeduncular circuits and lateral motivational/monoaminergic circuitry.
publicEvidence.limitations: Much evidence is animal; avoid labeling every habenular pathway anti-reward.

findings.originalValue: Superior hypophyseal and anterior communicating branches superiorly; internal carotid and posterior communicating branches inferiorly (segmental supply underlies chiasmal infarction).
findings.proposedReplacement: Variable contributions from superior hypophyseal, posterior communicating, anterior cerebral, and anterior communicating branches. Human dissections show important inferior pial supply from superior hypophyseal and posterior communicating arteries, with superior pial contributions and territorial overlap.
findings.explanation: Rigid superior-SHA/inferior-ICA assignment is false. Human dissection shows SHA as principal inferior pial contributor and overlapping superior input. No rigid segmental map follows.

textbookEvidence.supportSummary: Rigid superior-SHA/inferior-ICA assignment is false. Human dissection shows SHA as principal inferior pial contributor and overlapping superior input. No rigid segmental map follows.

publicEvidence.title: Salaud et al.2018, Optic-chiasm extrinsic/intrinsic supply
publicEvidence.evidenceType: Primary human dissection:13 specimens, microCT subset
publicEvidence.supportSummary: Inferior pial supply received SHA in13/13 and PCoA in12/13; superior supply also received SHA variably with ACA/AComA. Intrinsic supply was principally inferior.
publicEvidence.limitations: Small cadaveric sample; retain variable contributions and overlap.

findings.originalValue: Germinomas and pineal parenchymal tumors compress the pretectal plate and aqueduct — upgaze palsy, light-near dissociation, lid retraction, convergence-retraction nystagmus (Parinaud syndrome) with hydrocephalus; see the syndrome browser entry.
findings.proposedReplacement: Germinomas and pineal parenchymal tumors may compress dorsal midbrain and/or cerebral aqueduct. Dorsal involvement can produce some combination of upgaze paresis, light-near dissociation, lid retraction, and convergence-retraction nystagmus (Parinaud pattern); aqueduct obstruction can cause hydrocephalus. Findings depend on tumor extent.
findings.explanation: Complete ocular tetrad with hydrocephalus is presented as inevitable, unlike corrected syndrome card. Book explicitly says all Parinaud signs are not present in every case.

textbookEvidence.supportSummary: Complete ocular tetrad with hydrocephalus is presented as inevitable, unlike corrected syndrome card. Book explicitly says all Parinaud signs are not present in every case.

publicEvidence.title: Rousselle et al.2014/2015, Pineal region clinical symptoms
publicEvidence.supportSummary: Course depends on tumor type/extension; raised-pressure, ocular motor and endocrine findings vary. No universal complete tetrad or fixed symptom sequence.

findings.originalValue: Masses at the posterior third ventricle obstruct the cerebral aqueduct, causing headache, papilledema and gait failure before focal signs.
findings.proposedReplacement: A mass near the posterior third ventricle may obstruct the cerebral aqueduct, causing hydrocephalus with headache, nausea/vomiting, papilledema, or other raised-pressure findings. Ocular motor or other focal signs may coexist; no fixed symptom order is established.
findings.explanation: Original imposes gait failure and raised-pressure signs before focal signs. No universal sequence is supported.

textbookEvidence.supportSummary: Original imposes gait failure and raised-pressure signs before focal signs. No universal sequence is supported.

publicEvidence.title: Rousselle et al.2014/2015, Pineal region clinical symptoms
publicEvidence.supportSummary: Course depends on tumor type/extension; raised-pressure, ocular motor and endocrine findings vary. No universal complete tetrad or fixed symptom sequence.

findings.originalValue: Fastigial or vermal lesions give a wide-based staggering gait with truncal instability and nystagmus while limb coordination on the bed may be preserved; bilateral posterior fossa lesions therefore present predominantly as gait ataxia.
findings.proposedReplacement: Medial cerebellar/fastigial and vestibular circuit lesions can cause truncal or gait instability and ocular motor abnormalities, with limb coordination relatively spared when hemispheric pathways are preserved. Intermediate/lateral circuit extension can add limb ataxia; bilateral posterior-fossa location alone does not define a predominantly gait syndrome.
findings.explanation: Medial trunk versus lateral limb localization is supported; original conclusion about all bilateral posterior-fossa lesions is too broad.

textbookEvidence.supportSummary: Medial trunk versus lateral limb localization is supported; original conclusion about all bilateral posterior-fossa lesions is too broad.

publicEvidence.title: Ilg et al.2008, Focal cerebellar lesions and gait
publicEvidence.evidenceType: Primary human lesion-symptom study:12 chronic patients
publicEvidence.supportSummary: Distinguishes medial balance-related deficits from limb coordination/gait adaptation associated with other involved cerebellar structures.
publicEvidence.limitations: Selected post-resection cohort; bilateral posterior-fossa location alone does not define phenotype.

findings.originalValue: Small posterior-limb/genu infarcts give contralateral face-arm-leg weakness without cortical signs; larger capsular strokes add dense hemisensory loss and dysarthria-clumsy-hand syndrome.
findings.proposedReplacement: Small posterior-limb or genu infarcts can cause contralateral weakness or dysarthria without cortical signs. Sensory loss, ataxic hemiparesis, or dysarthria-clumsy hand depend on involved pathways; dysarthria-clumsy hand itself can be a lacunar capsular syndrome.
findings.explanation: Original reserves DCH for larger strokes. Human registry includes predominantly lacunar lesions; textbook Table10.3 includes several small capsular pathway syndromes.

textbookEvidence.supportSummary: Original reserves DCH for larger strokes. Human registry includes predominantly lacunar lesions; textbook Table10.3 includes several small capsular pathway syndromes.

publicEvidence.title: Arboix et al.2004,35 dysarthria-clumsy hand patients
publicEvidence.supportSummary: 33/35 cases supported the lacunar hypothesis; internal capsule was a frequent site. DCH is not restricted to larger capsular strokes.

findings.originalValue: Contralateral incongruous homonymous hemianopia from anterior-choroidal-territory infarction of the optic radiations.
findings.proposedReplacement: Retrolenticular optic-radiation injury can cause contralateral homonymous visual-field loss. Completeness and congruity depend on affected fibers and lesion extent; incongruity is not obligatory. Vascular supply is variable.
findings.explanation: Original requires incongruous hemianopia and one arterial source. Book describes congruity as tendency; human series includes many congruent radiation defects.

textbookEvidence.supportSummary: Original requires incongruous hemianopia and one arterial source. Book describes congruity as tendency; human series includes many congruent radiation defects.

publicEvidence.title: Kedar et al.2007, Congruency in homonymous hemianopia
publicEvidence.supportSummary: Many optic-radiation lesions produced congruent homonymous defects. Incongruity is not an obligatory feature of radiation injury.

findings.originalValue: Progressive caudate volume loss underlies chorea and frontal-executive decline — visible on the coronal context silhouettes.
findings.proposedReplacement: Huntington disease involves progressive striatal degeneration, including caudate and putamen, with motor, cognitive, and behavioral manifestations and additional brain involvement. Caudate atrophy may be evident on patient CT or MRI; the invariant atlas silhouette does not demonstrate disease-related volume loss.
findings.explanation: Supported disease association is paired with false claim that progressive atrophy is visible on static coronal context silhouettes. Book refers to patient CT/MRI and includes putamen/cortical involvement.

textbookEvidence.supportSummary: Supported disease association is paired with false claim that progressive atrophy is visible on static coronal context silhouettes. Book refers to patient CT/MRI and includes putamen/cortical involvement.

publicEvidence.title: Reiner et al.2011, Huntington disease neuropathology
publicEvidence.supportSummary: Striatal caudate/putamen projection-neuron degeneration and other brain involvement are described. Actual atrophy requires patient imaging/pathology.
publicEvidence.limitations: Static-atlas display limitation is also established by application inspection; no patient-specific disease input exists.

retainedLimitations: No clinical accuracy certification or diagnostic validation; cases describe possible localization patterns, not obligatory presentations.
No patient/template registration, stereotactic coordinate, boundary/volume or exact fiber-trajectory validation. Qualitative figures do not justify numerical corrections.
Construction laterality drives drawing duplication. For paired IV/XII/IML correct anatomicalLaterality separately and disclose compressed central proxy; no fabricated offsets.
Oculomotor and EW laterality/subdivision issues are nuanced; no simplistic metadata change proposed.
Inferior vestibular region tag and optic-chiasm level selectors retain taxonomy/geometry ambiguity needing safe independent display decisions.
Tiny nuclear perfusion is variable and often absent from textbook; broad regional supply reviewed without certifying every microscopic territory.
Telencephalic/cerebellar context shapes in these files are application grouping, not developmental membership.
Habenular, DMH, red-nuclear and other models often rely on animals; no upgrade to precise proven human circuits.
All26 syndrome cards reread; eponyms overlap and rare variants exist. No additional supported syndrome-card correction identified.
Book text/figures remain outside repository in private scratch inspection; none redistributed into app.
